Orochi framework.long:
Orochi is a contemporary trading framework sold by subscription, built from five components: auction market theory, TPO and volume profile, Elliott Wave, VWAP, and order flow. It positions itself against the ICT vocabulary, arguing that most retail traders chase indicators and setups without understanding the auction underneath.

The components are not new, and that is the useful thing to notice. Auction market theory and market profile come from Steidlmayer's work at the CBOT in the 1980s; Elliott Wave dates to the 1930s; VWAP and order flow are execution tools institutions have used for decades. The framework is an assembly of existing material, which is not a criticism — it is how most frameworks are built — but it means the components can be evaluated separately, and several of them already have been.

Four of the five need tick or full-depth data to test properly, which is not available at retail without paying for it. The fifth, VWAP reversion, was tested in this project's own companion engine and failed: after correcting an independent bootstrap to a block bootstrap on overlapping windows, the effective sample fell to roughly three observations and the hard gate refused it outright for insufficient data.

Where people get fooled: the marketing claims the framework does not suffer the alpha decay that affects strategies. That claim cannot be wrong in any way you could check, which is what makes it worth distrusting rather than believing — an approach immune to decay is also an approach immune to measurement. Ask what result would count as it failing.
Orochi framework.usage: Generally encountered as a paid community teaching auction-based order flow; evaluate the five components separately, since most of them predate it by decades.

Turtle system.long:
The Turtle system is Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt's 1980s trend-following experiment. Dennis believed trading could be taught; Eckhardt did not. They recruited a group, taught them a mechanical rule set, and funded them. The core is a Donchian breakout: enter when price makes a 20-day extreme, exit when it makes a 10-day extreme the other way, size positions from volatility, and pyramid into winners.

What makes it unusual is that the rules were eventually published in full. Almost nothing else in retail trading can be tested exactly as its author specified — most frameworks leave the decisive detail vague, which is what makes them untestable. The Turtle rules do not. You can code them, run them, and get the same answer the authors would.

That testability has produced an honest and uncomfortable record. The approach worked in the commodity markets of its era; published trend-following results since have been far more modest, and the long flat stretches are severe. Trend following also loses on most of its trades by design — its return comes from a small number of very large winners, which is psychologically the hardest shape to sit through.

Where people get fooled: the story does the persuading. A bet between two traders, recruits pulled from nowhere, a large headline profit — it is a good story, and stories are the least reliable evidence there is. The rules are the valuable part precisely because they can be checked without the story.
Turtle system.usage: Typically cited as the origin of retail trend following; unusually, its published rules can be backtested exactly as specified.

Connors RSI-2.long:
Larry Connors' RSI-2 is a mean-reversion rule: take a 2-period RSI rather than the conventional 14, wait for it to reach an extreme while price sits above a long moving average, and exit when price crosses back above a shorter one. The short lookback makes the oscillator far twitchier than the standard setting, which is the point — it is measuring a brief stretch, not a trend.

It was published in Street Smarts (1996, written with Linda Raschke) and developed further in Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (2008), with backtests produced alongside Cesar Alvarez. Publication is the strength here: the rule is specific enough to code, and specific rules can be argued with.

The long-moving-average filter is doing more work than the oscillator. It restricts the rule to buying dips inside uptrends, which is a structurally different bet from buying dips generally, and removing it changes the results substantially. Anyone testing this should test the filter separately before crediting the RSI.

Where people get fooled: the strategy is famous for its win rate, and the win rate is the least informative number attached to it. Mean-reversion rules of this shape produce many small winners and occasional large losers, so a high proportion of winning trades is what the design produces rather than evidence that it earns anything. This project's own engine found the family losing across every variant that accumulated a real sample, while the proportion of winning trades stayed high throughout. Read expectancy instead.
Connors RSI-2.usage: Generally quoted as the canonical short-term mean-reversion rule; the trend filter matters more than the oscillator, and win rate is the wrong column to read.

Darvas box.long:
Nicolas Darvas's method, from the 1950s, draws a box around a consolidation: the recent high forms the ceiling and the recent low the floor. A close above the ceiling is the entry, the stop sits under the floor, and as price steps into a new box the stop trails up behind it.

Stripped of the story it is a breakout rule with a mechanical trailing stop, and a fairly clean one. The box gives an objective definition of a range — no judgement about whether the consolidation looks right — and the trailing rule is specified rather than left to feel. Those two properties make it testable, which puts it ahead of most named methods.

Darvas was a touring ballroom dancer who traded by telegram, receiving weekly quotes while abroad. That constraint is the genuinely interesting part: it forced long holding periods and removed the ability to react intraday, which is closer to how a retail trader can actually operate than most day-trading material.

Where people get fooled: the two million dollars in the book's title is the book's own claim and was never independently audited, and the era matters — a concentrated bull market in a handful of names is the most forgiving possible environment for a breakout-and-trail rule. Treat the method as a specification worth testing, and the fortune as marketing that has been repeated for seventy years.
Darvas box.usage: Typically used as an objective breakout-and-trail specification; the box gives a mechanical range definition that most pattern methods lack.

Dual momentum.long:
Gary Antonacci's dual momentum, set out in Dual Momentum Investing (2014), combines two rules. Relative momentum picks whichever of a small set of assets has performed best over a lookback. Absolute momentum then checks that the chosen asset has beaten cash or short-term bills over the same window, and moves to cash if it has not.

The two halves do different jobs, and the second is the important one. Relative momentum only ever says which of your options is least bad — during a broad decline it will happily hold the best-performing falling asset. Absolute momentum is what takes the position off entirely, and it is where the drawdown reduction comes from.

Both rest on the momentum premium, which is among the better-documented anomalies and one of the few where post-publication decay has been hard to detect. It rebalances monthly, so costs stay small relative to the holding period — unusual among named systems.

Where people get fooled: the lookback is a parameter, and the results move with it. A rule that works at twelve months and fails at nine has found the sample rather than the effect, so the honest test is whether a neighbourhood of lookbacks behaves similarly, not whether one of them looks impressive. Momentum also delivers its worst stretches exactly at turning points, when it is holding what has been winning right as that stops being true.
Dual momentum.usage: Generally run monthly over a handful of asset classes; the absolute-momentum filter is what changes the drawdown profile, not the asset selection.

Pairs trading.long:
Pairs trading takes two instruments whose prices have historically moved together, waits for the spread between them to stretch, then shorts the strong one and buys the weak one — betting the relationship reasserts itself rather than betting on direction.

It has real academic standing. Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst documented the approach in the Review of Financial Studies in 2006, testing a simple distance rule across four decades of daily data. Because the position is long one thing and short another of similar size, broad market moves largely cancel, which is why the approach is described as market-neutral.

The risk is not the market — it is that the relationship was never structural in the first place. Two instruments can correlate for years because both respond to the same conditions, then decouple permanently when one company's circumstances change. A spread trade against a broken relationship does not revert; it just keeps widening, and the short leg has no ceiling.

Where people get fooled: finding pairs is a search, and searching thousands of combinations for the ones that historically co-moved is exactly the procedure that manufactures relationships out of noise. The more pairs you screen, the more spurious ones you will find, and the co-movement you selected on is the least likely part to persist. Any pair worth trading should have a reason two businesses move together that you could state before running the screen.
Pairs trading.usage: Typically run as a market-neutral spread on instruments with a structural link; the screen that finds the pair is where most of the false positives are created.

Statistical arbitrage.long:
Statistical arbitrage runs a large number of positions, each with only a very slight expected advantage, and relies on breadth rather than accuracy. No individual position is expected to be reliable; the portfolio is expected to be, because averaging many weak independent bets produces a far steadier result than any one of them.

The arithmetic is the law of large numbers doing the work. A tiny edge repeated across thousands of positions becomes measurable, provided the positions are genuinely independent and the costs per position are small enough not to consume the edge. Both conditions are demanding, and the second is where retail participation ends.

That is the honest structural point. The edges involved are typically far smaller than the spread and commission a retail account pays per trade, so the same strategy that is profitable at institutional cost levels is reliably unprofitable at retail ones. The infrastructure — colocation, direct feeds, execution algorithms — exists to push costs below the edge, not because it is impressive.

Where people get fooled: assuming the barrier is knowing the technique. The technique is well described in public; the barrier is cost per trade and the independence assumption. Positions that look independent in calm conditions correlate sharply in stressed ones, which is when a book of thousands of small bets stops behaving like thousands and starts behaving like one.
Statistical arbitrage.usage: Generally institutional: it needs breadth, independence and per-trade costs far below what a retail account pays.
